attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post. It is not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'That they would be' slightly narrows assurances that hallucinations were prevented or would be solved, but this does not change what is scored.

contract.note: An ordinary plain reading: hallucinations still persist and repeated assurances existed. It does not demand that rates never improved or that every provider made promises.

evidence.note: Feb 27, 2025 system card. OpenAI reports a 19% PersonQA hallucination rate for its newest model and says more work is needed. This is a company disclosure, but it goes against the company's interest and falls inside the target month.

Independent research recording 2023 assurances from legal-AI vendors that hallucinations were largely prevented or eliminated. This supports the assurances component. Its 2024 failure findings are context only.
The launch post only expects fewer hallucinations. It qualifies the assurances but does not show that hallucinations were solved.

reviews.rationale: In February 2025 OpenAI's own evaluation showed substantial remaining hallucination rates. Nothing in the packet shows a broadly effective fix. Independent research documents repeated vendor assurances from 2023 that hallucinations were prevented or solved. Both parts of the plain reading hold.

attribution.note: Marcus's own bullet in his own post.

semantics.note: The 'should' only states an AGI requirement. In context ('what we have... still missing'), the claim describes current systems, and 'often' is kept.

contract.note: The plain reading (recurring structural errors in contemporary general-purpose models) is ordinary. However, no threshold or model set is given, so the result depends on the evaluator's operational choices.

evidence.note: January 2025 COLING paper on composition in embedding models. It tests embeddings rather than conversational models and leaves the theory-mismatch explanation open.
2024 preprint showing hierarchical generalization in small transformers trained from scratch. It falls outside the target window and does not cover deployed models.

reviews.rationale: No independent controlled evaluation of contemporary general-purpose models in early 2025 is in the packet. One item covers embeddings and the other covers small from-scratch models. Neither establishes nor refutes recurring structural errors in current systems.

attribution.note: Marcus's own footnote in his own post.

semantics.note: Mostly faithful. 'Arithmetic' is a bit broader than the multiplication study the footnote refers to, and 'o1' is ambiguous between variants. The contract correctly narrows both.

contract.note: Tying the claim to the linked September 2024 study of o1-mini and o1-preview, and reading 'wildly unreliable' as recurring exact-answer errors at larger operand sizes, is a fair plain reading.

evidence.note: The evaluator's thread shows decent accuracy only up to about 9x9 on a test that runs to 20x20, with o1-mini and o1-preview similar. Improvement over GPT-4o does not establish reliability.
News report of the same evaluation: o1 gets 9x9 products right about half the time. This is substantial unreliability.
OpenAI discloses that o1-mini was optimized for STEM, which is consistent with the 'augmentation' premise. It is not an outcome measure.
GNU bc manual dated 2001 documents arbitrary-precision multiplication. This supports the 'handled for decades' component.
GMP's project page dates its first release to 1991 for arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic. This supports the historical comparison.

reviews.rationale: The cited evaluation shows o1 variants failing often beyond roughly 9x9 digits (about half correct at 9x9) on a test reaching 20x20, despite STEM specialization. Arbitrary-precision software from 1991 and 2001 handled these operations exactly. Both components hold under the contract.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful conjunction: the GPT-5 project became GPT-4.5, it failed, and it followed more than two years of costly work.

contract.note: Reading 'fail' as missing the intended capability leap, not shipping nothing, is ordinary and fair. Start date and spending are not specified, so the duration component depends on the evaluator's evidence.

evidence.note: WSJ reporting from anonymous sources: Orion was the GPT-5 effort, ran behind expectations, and was very expensive. Its start date of March 2023 gives just under two years by the release, so the duration is not established.
Secondary reproduction of Altman's statement linking Orion to GPT-4.5. This supports the relabeling component only.
The GPT-4.5 release shows improvements over GPT-4o. This rules out a reading of total failure but does not show the original targets were met.

reviews.rationale: Three components are supported: the identity link, missed expectations, and high cost (from reporting). The essential 'more than two years' component is not established. The reported start of March 2023 gives just under two years, but earlier work is not excluded. Nothing is refuted, so the conjunction stays unresolved.
